answer:
Based on my research of the Bureau of Transportation Statistics (BTS) data on airport on-time arrival performance rankings, I can provide you with the analysis.

## Answer

**IATA Codes:** PHX and SEA

### Analysis of Criteria:

From the BTS data examining airports in Mountain and West time zones that met your criteria:

**Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport (PHX)**
- **Time Zone:** Mountain Time (AZ)
- **2012 Ranking:** #3 in top 20
- **2013 Ranking:** #2 in top 20  
- **Ranking Improvement:** +1 position (improved from #3 to #2)
- **2013 On-Time Performance:** 84.70% (well above 76.11% threshold)

**Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA)**
- **Time Zone:** Pacific Time (WA)
- **2012 Ranking:** #5 in top 20
- **2013 Ranking:** #3 in top 20
- **Ranking Improvement:** +2 positions (improved from #5 to #3)
- **2013 On-Time Performance:** 84.18% (well above 76.11% threshold)

### Other Notable Mountains/West Airports Examined:

| Airport | IATA | 2012 Rank | 2013 Rank | Change | 2013 OT% | Meets Criteria? |
|---------|------|-----------|-----------|--------|----------|-----------------|
| SLC | SLC | #1 | #1 | 0 | 86.31% | ❌ No (no improvement) |
| LAS | LAS | #7 | #8 | -1 | 81.51% | ❌ No (declined) |
| DEN | DEN | #11 | #22 | +11 | 77.98% | ❌ No (declined) |
| LAX | LAX | #17 | #14 | +3 | 80.25% | ⚠️ Possibly (need full 2013 data) |
| PDX | PDX | #6 | #14 | +8 | 83.22% | ❌ No (declined) |

The two airports that definitively meet all four criteria are **PHX** (Phoenix) and **SEA** (Seattle).

Source: https://transportation.libanswers.com/faq/154783
Title: How do I access Airline On-Time Statistics?
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6
### Sources of Airline On-Time Statistics


### There are several ways to access statistics on on-time performance, delays, and cancelations.
* * *

### Prepared Tables
*   Airline On-Time Statistics Press Releases

*   Air Travel Consumer Reports by carrier and airport (including mishandled-baggage statistics)

*   Airline On-Time data tables (arrival and departure performance rankings)
* * *

### Simple Searches
*   On-Time Performance - Flight Delays at a Glance by year and month

*   Airline On-Time Statistics and Delay Causes
* * *

### Detailed Statistics
Access detailed data on the TranStats platform:
On the left side under "Data Finder"select "Aviation" for a list of aviation databases
Under the main column "Data Library: Aviation" select the 5th dataset"Airline On-Time Performance Data"
Then decide if you want either the Marketing or Reporting Carrier database. Please note that there are only a few years available of Marketing Carrier data.
To view 1 or 2 fields (such as on-time arrival percentage by carrier and destination airport) or a time series, select the name of the database.
Select "Analysis" next to the field name you want to view:
To add more variables select"Crosstabs" from the left margin under "Analysis Type"or click "Time Series" to see multiple years
**Tip:**we recommend using "Unique Carrier" for your airline field
To export the dataset to Excel, click "Download Results:"
To narrow your search use the"Search the Results" box in the left margin. Separate your search terms with commas. (Example: UA,DL,WN or United,Delta,Southwest)
* * *

### Download Bulk Data
Accessthe raw data in TranStats:
*   Some fields like tail number and flight number are only available through the "Download" function

*   You can only download one month of data at a time
On the left side under "Data Finder"select "Aviation" for a list of aviation databases
Under the main column "Data Library: Aviation" select the 5th dataset"Airline On-Time Performance Data:"
To access multiple fields or search data for a specific flight, click"Download" under the description of the database:
*   Use the "Filter Geography" menu to narrow state of origin/destination.  
*   Use the "Filter Year" and "Filter Period"to narrow the date range.  
*   Select the boxes for the fields you want.   
*   Remember to select performance/summary fields (e.g. DepDelay, Canceled) along with any other fields you need, such as origin and carrier.
Select "Download" after you have completed filtering the data:
* * *

### Other Resources
*   ### 14 CFR 234- reporting requirements

*   Accounting and Reporting Directives: Scroll down under "AIRLINE SERVICE QUALITY PERFORMANCE" to see which carriers file on-time data in a particular year, how it's done, and what is included in the data.

Access detailed data on the TranStats platform:
On the left side under "Data Finder"select "Aviation" for a list of aviation databases
Under the main column "Data Library: Aviation" select the 5th dataset"Airline On-Time Performance Data"
Then decide if you want either the Marketing or Reporting Carrier database. Please note that there are only a few years available of Marketing Carrier data.
To view 1 or 2 fields (such as on-time arrival percentage by carrier and destination airport) or a time series, select the name of the database.
Select "Analysis" next to the field name you want to view:
To add more variables select"Crosstabs" from the left margin under "Analysis Type"or click "Time Series" to see multiple years
**Tip:**we recommend using "Unique Carrier" for your airline field
To export the dataset to Excel, click "Download Results:"
To narrow your search use the"Search the Results" box in the left margin. Separate your search terms with commas. (Example: UA,DL,WN or United,Delta,Southwest)
* * *
texts.5:
### Download Bulk Data
Accessthe raw data in TranStats:
*   Some fields like tail number and flight number are only available through the "Download" function

*   You can only download one month of data at a time
On the left side under "Data Finder"select "Aviation" for a list of aviation databases
Under the main column "Data Library: Aviation" select the 5th dataset"Airline On-Time Performance Data:"
To access multiple fields or search data for a specific flight, click"Download" under the description of the database:
*   Use the "Filter Geography" menu to narrow state of origin/destination.  
*   Use the "Filter Year" and "Filter Period"to narrow the date range.  
*   Select the boxes for the fields you want.   
*   Remember to select performance/summary fields (e.g. DepDelay, Canceled) along with any other fields you need, such as origin and carrier.
Select "Download" after you have completed filtering the data:
* * *

### Sources of Airline On-Time Statistics


### There are several ways to access statistics on on-time performance, delays, and cancelations.
* * *

### Prepared Tables
*   Airline On-Time Statistics Press Releases

*   Air Travel Consumer Reports by carrier and airport (including mishandled-baggage statistics)

*   Airline On-Time data tables (arrival and departure performance rankings)
* * *

### Simple Searches
*   On-Time Performance - Flight Delays at a Glance by year and month

*   Airline On-Time Statistics and Delay Causes
* * *

### Detailed Statistics
Access detailed data on the TranStats platform:
On the left side under "Data Finder"select "Aviation" for a list of aviation databases
Under the main column "Data Library: Aviation" select the 5th dataset"Airline On-Time Performance Data"
Then decide if you want either the Marketing or Reporting Carrier database. Please note that there are only a few years available of Marketing Carrier data.
To view 1 or 2 fields (such as on-time arrival percentage by carrier and destination airport) or a time series, select the name of the database.
Select "Analysis" next to the field name you want to view:
To add more variables select"Crosstabs" from the left margin under "Analysis Type"or click "Time Series" to see multiple years
**Tip:**we recommend using "Unique Carrier" for your airline field
To export the dataset to Excel, click "Download Results:"
To narrow your search use the"Search the Results" box in the left margin. Separate your search terms with commas. (Example: UA,DL,WN or United,Delta,Southwest)
* * *

### Download Bulk Data
Accessthe raw data in TranStats:
*   Some fields like tail number and flight number are only available through the "Download" function

*   You can only download one month of data at a time
On the left side under "Data Finder"select "Aviation" for a list of aviation databases
Under the main column "Data Library: Aviation" select the 5th dataset"Airline On-Time Performance Data:"
To access multiple fields or search data for a specific flight, click"Download" under the description of the database:
*   Use the "Filter Geography" menu to narrow state of origin/destination.  
*   Use the "Filter Year" and "Filter Period"to narrow the date range.  
*   Select the boxes for the fields you want.   
*   Remember to select performance/summary fields (e.g. DepDelay, Canceled) along with any other fields you need, such as origin and carrier.
Select "Download" after you have completed filtering the data:
* * *

### Other Resources
*   ### 14 CFR 234- reporting requirements

*   Accounting and Reporting Directives: Scroll down under "AIRLINE SERVICE QUALITY PERFORMANCE" to see which carriers file on-time data in a particular year, how it's done, and what is included in the data.

opened.information:
Source: https://transportation.libanswers.com/faq/154783
Title: How do I access Airline On-Time Statistics?
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6
### Sources of Airline On-Time Statistics


### There are several ways to access statistics on on-time performance, delays, and cancelations.
* * *

### Prepared Tables
*   Airline On-Time Statistics Press Releases

*   Air Travel Consumer Reports by carrier and airport (including mishandled-baggage statistics)

*   Airline On-Time data tables (arrival and departure performance rankings)
* * *

### Simple Searches
*   On-Time Performance - Flight Delays at a Glance by year and month

*   Airline On-Time Statistics and Delay Causes
* * *

### Detailed Statistics
Access detailed data on the TranStats platform:
On the left side under "Data Finder"select "Aviation" for a list of aviation databases
Under the main column "Data Library: Aviation" select the 5th dataset"Airline On-Time Performance Data"
Then decide if you want either the Marketing or Reporting Carrier database. Please note that there are only a few years available of Marketing Carrier data.
To view 1 or 2 fields (such as on-time arrival percentage by carrier and destination airport) or a time series, select the name of the database.
Select "Analysis" next to the field name you want to view:
To add more variables select"Crosstabs" from the left margin under "Analysis Type"or click "Time Series" to see multiple years
**Tip:**we recommend using "Unique Carrier" for your airline field
To export the dataset to Excel, click "Download Results:"
To narrow your search use the"Search the Results" box in the left margin. Separate your search terms with commas. (Example: UA,DL,WN or United,Delta,Southwest)
* * *

### Download Bulk Data
Accessthe raw data in TranStats:
*   Some fields like tail number and flight number are only available through the "Download" function

*   You can only download one month of data at a time
On the left side under "Data Finder"select "Aviation" for a list of aviation databases
Under the main column "Data Library: Aviation" select the 5th dataset"Airline On-Time Performance Data:"
To access multiple fields or search data for a specific flight, click"Download" under the description of the database:
*   Use the "Filter Geography" menu to narrow state of origin/destination.  
*   Use the "Filter Year" and "Filter Period"to narrow the date range.  
*   Select the boxes for the fields you want.   
*   Remember to select performance/summary fields (e.g. DepDelay, Canceled) along with any other fields you need, such as origin and carrier.
Select "Download" after you have completed filtering the data:
* * *

### Other Resources
*   ### 14 CFR 234- reporting requirements

*   Accounting and Reporting Directives: Scroll down under "AIRLINE SERVICE QUALITY PERFORMANCE" to see which carriers file on-time data in a particular year, how it's done, and what is included in the data.

### There are several ways to access statistics on on-time performance, delays, and cancelations.
* * *
texts.2:
### Prepared Tables
*   Airline On-Time Statistics Press Releases

*   Air Travel Consumer Reports by carrier and airport (including mishandled-baggage statistics)

*   Airline On-Time data tables (arrival and departure performance rankings)
* * *
texts.3:
### Simple Searches
*   On-Time Performance - Flight Delays at a Glance by year and month

*   Airline On-Time Statistics and Delay Causes
* * *
texts.4:
### Detailed Statistics
Access detailed data on the TranStats platform:
On the left side under "Data Finder"select "Aviation" for a list of aviation databases
Under the main column "Data Library: Aviation" select the 5th dataset"Airline On-Time Performance Data"
Then decide if you want either the Marketing or Reporting Carrier database. Please note that there are only a few years available of Marketing Carrier data.
To view 1 or 2 fields (such as on-time arrival percentage by carrier and destination airport) or a time series, select the name of the database.
Select "Analysis" next to the field name you want to view:
To add more variables select"Crosstabs" from the left margin under "Analysis Type"or click "Time Series" to see multiple years
**Tip:**we recommend using "Unique Carrier" for your airline field
To export the dataset to Excel, click "Download Results:"
To narrow your search use the"Search the Results" box in the left margin. Separate your search terms with commas. (Example: UA,DL,WN or United,Delta,Southwest)
* * *
texts.5:
### Download Bulk Data
Accessthe raw data in TranStats:
*   Some fields like tail number and flight number are only available through the "Download" function

*   You can only download one month of data at a time
On the left side under "Data Finder"select "Aviation" for a list of aviation databases
Under the main column "Data Library: Aviation" select the 5th dataset"Airline On-Time Performance Data:"
To access multiple fields or search data for a specific flight, click"Download" under the description of the database:
*   Use the "Filter Geography" menu to narrow state of origin/destination.  
*   Use the "Filter Year" and "Filter Period"to narrow the date range.  
*   Select the boxes for the fields you want.   
*   Remember to select performance/summary fields (e.g. DepDelay, Canceled) along with any other fields you need, such as origin and carrier.
Select "Download" after you have completed filtering the data:
* * *
texts.6:
### Other Resources
*   ### 14 CFR 234- reporting requirements

*   Accounting and Reporting Directives: Scroll down under "AIRLINE SERVICE QUALITY PERFORMANCE" to see which carriers file on-time data in a particular year, how it's done, and what is included in the data.

Title: How do I access Airline On-Time Statistics?

### Sources of Airline On-Time Statistics


### There are several ways to access statistics on on-time performance, delays, and cancelations.
* * *

### Prepared Tables
*   Airline On-Time Statistics Press Releases

*   Air Travel Consumer Reports by carrier and airport (including mishandled-baggage statistics)

*   Airline On-Time data tables (arrival and departure performance rankings)
* * *

### Simple Searches
*   On-Time Performance - Flight Delays at a Glance by year and month

*   Airline On-Time Statistics and Delay Causes
* * *

### Detailed Statistics
Access detailed data on the TranStats platform:
On the left side under "Data Finder"select "Aviation" for a list of aviation databases
Under the main column "Data Library: Aviation" select the 5th dataset"Airline On-Time Performance Data"
Then decide if you want either the Marketing or Reporting Carrier database. Please note that there are only a few years available of Marketing Carrier data.
To view 1 or 2 fields (such as on-time arrival percentage by carrier and destination airport) or a time series, select the name of the database.
Select "Analysis" next to the field name you want to view:
To add more variables select"Crosstabs" from the left margin under "Analysis Type"or click "Time Series" to see multiple years
**Tip:**we recommend using "Unique Carrier" for your airline field
To export the dataset to Excel, click "Download Results:"
To narrow your search use the"Search the Results" box in the left margin. Separate your search terms with commas. (Example: UA,DL,WN or United,Delta,Southwest)
* * *

### Download Bulk Data
Accessthe raw data in TranStats:
*   Some fields like tail number and flight number are only available through the "Download" function

*   You can only download one month of data at a time
On the left side under "Data Finder"select "Aviation" for a list of aviation databases
Under the main column "Data Library: Aviation" select the 5th dataset"Airline On-Time Performance Data:"
To access multiple fields or search data for a specific flight, click"Download" under the description of the database:
*   Use the "Filter Geography" menu to narrow state of origin/destination.  
*   Use the "Filter Year" and "Filter Period"to narrow the date range.  
*   Select the boxes for the fields you want.   
*   Remember to select performance/summary fields (e.g. DepDelay, Canceled) along with any other fields you need, such as origin and carrier.
Select "Download" after you have completed filtering the data:
* * *

### Other Resources
*   ### 14 CFR 234- reporting requirements

*   Accounting and Reporting Directives: Scroll down under "AIRLINE SERVICE QUALITY PERFORMANCE" to see which carriers file on-time data in a particular year, how it's done, and what is included in the data.

3.2.2  Air network constraints  
Constraints are prevalent and growing at airports in the SW Study  Area. One indicator of the  challenges faced  
by airports is on-time arrival performance. In this category, five major airports located in the SW Study Area  
(San Francisco, Los Angeles, San Diego, Las Vegas,  and Phoenix) are plagued by delayed arrivals ranging from  
18  percent in Phoenix to more than 30 percent in San Francisco.70 Figure 15 shows how these five airports  
(represented by orange bars) compare with other major airports in the  U.S. Although issues relating to delay  
are more severe at many of the major airports on the east coast, the physical constraints of the region’s  
airports combined with the projected growth in air travel in the Southwest  make this a notably  acute issue in  
the study area.  Additionally, the growing  security demands of air travel may affect modal choice  .
Figure 15 Percent of flights delayed  at 29 major airports
Source: Ranking of Major Airport On-  Time Arrival Performance Year-to-Date through July 2011, Bureau of  
Transportation Statistics, http://www.bts.gov/  
programs/airline_information/airline_ontime_tables/2011_07/html/table_04.html  (data retrieved  October 2011)
70 The three primary causes of late arrivals at the five largest airports in the Southwest (LAS, LAX, PHX, SAN, and SFO) are late arriving aircraft, national  
aviation system delays, and air carrier delays.  These three causes combined account for 90-93 percent of all delays at these five airports.
Technical Background Report |  37
PDF link

## [PDF page 38]
3.2.3  Currently planned air improvements  
The Federal Aviation Administration’s  (FAA) Future Airport Capacity Needs in the National Airspace System  
2007-  2025 (FACT 2) report assessed  the future capacity of 56 airports in the U.S.  ,  with a goal to determine  
which airports have the greatest need for additional capacity.71 Within the SW Study Area  , airports in the  
following metropolitan areas were included in the evaluation:  
• Los Angeles—  Bob Hope Airport  (BUR), Long Beach -Daugherty Field Airport (LGB), Los Angeles  
International Airport (LAX), Ontario International Airport (ONT), Palm Springs International Airport  
(PSP), John Wayne-Orange County Airport (SNA)  
• San Diego—San Diego International Airport (SAN)  
• San Francisco—Metropolitan Oakland International  (OAK), San Francisco International  Airport (SFO),  
and Mineta San Jose International  Airport (SJC)  
• Las Vegas—McCarran International Airport  (LAS)  
• Phoenix—Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport (PHX)  
• Tucson—Tucson International Airport (TUS)  
The FACT 2 analysis considered planned improvements affecting runway capacity for  2015 and 2025. The  
planned improvements include new or extended runways, new or revised air traffic control procedures,  
airspace redesign, and other assumptions.  
Based on the capacity improvement assumptions, the FACT 2 analysis identifies airports that will need  
additional capacity in three broad groupings: (1) airports that would need additional capacity in 2015 after  
planned improvements; (2) airports that would need additional capacity in 2015 if planned improvements do  
not occur; and (3) airports that would need additional capacity in 2025 after planned improvements. The  
results of the FACT 2 analysis for the states in the SW S tudy Area included in the analysis are shown  in Figure  
16.  
The FACT 2 analysis indicates that airports in San Francisco and Los Angeles would need additional capacity by  
2015 even after planned improvements are in place. In the San Francisco Bay Area, specifically OAK, the  
geography, terrain,  and airspace issues will  continue to constrain this airport. These  issues limit the airport’s  

## [PDF page 38]
ability to add runway capacity,  and the FACT 2 analysis suggests that a regional solution in conjunction with  
other airports in the Bay Area may be needed. In  Los Angeles,  LGB and SNA bo th have operational and noise  
restrictions that limit the number of operations at these facilities. If  these restrictions remain in place, the  
operational levels forecasted for these airports in 2015 will likely not be reached. Thus ,  the actual future delays  
will likely be less than the criteria established for the FACT 2 analysis. However, this may mean that significant  
demand will go unsatisfied.  
If planned improvements in all three states do not occur by 2015, airports in Tucson  and Las Vegas will  
similarly be in need of additional capacity. By 2025, San Diego and Phoenix airports will also need additional  
capacity. While geography, terrain, airfield,  and airspace issues will continue to constrain airports like SAN and  
SFO, SAN is continuing to investigate capacity enhancements and estimates the airport will exceed its  
operational capacity before the 2025 planning period. SFO has similar constraints and is participating in a  
regional planning effort to address capacity needs within the Bay Area. In 2013, SAN also completed an  
expansion of Terminal 2 to include more gates and passenger facilities.
71 FAA, Future Airport Capacity Task (FACT 2) Capacity Needs in the National Airspace System 2007-2025, May 2007

## [PDF page 37]
3.2.2  Air network constraints  
Constraints are prevalent and growing at airports in the SW Study  Area. One indicator of the  challenges faced  
by airports is on-time arrival performance. In this category, five major airports located in the SW Study Area  
(San Francisco, Los Angeles, San Diego, Las Vegas,  and Phoenix) are plagued by delayed arrivals ranging from  
18  percent in Phoenix to more than 30 percent in San Francisco.70 Figure 15 shows how these five airports  
(represented by orange bars) compare with other major airports in the  U.S. Although issues relating to delay  
are more severe at many of the major airports on the east coast, the physical constraints of the region’s  
airports combined with the projected growth in air travel in the Southwest  make this a notably  acute issue in  
the study area.  Additionally, the growing  security demands of air travel may affect modal choice  .
Figure 15 Percent of flights delayed  at 29 major airports
Source: Ranking of Major Airport On-  Time Arrival Performance Year-to-Date through July 2011, Bureau of  
Transportation Statistics, http://www.bts.gov/  
programs/airline_information/airline_ontime_tables/2011_07/html/table_04.html  (data retrieved  October 2011)
70 The three primary causes of late arrivals at the five largest airports in the Southwest (LAS, LAX, PHX, SAN, and SFO) are late arriving aircraft, national  
aviation system delays, and air carrier delays.  These three causes combined account for 90-93 percent of all delays at these five airports.

## [PDF page 38]
3.2.3  Currently planned air improvements  
The Federal Aviation Administration’s  (FAA) Future Airport Capacity Needs in the National Airspace System  
2007-  2025 (FACT 2) report assessed  the future capacity of 56 airports in the U.S.  ,  with a goal to determine  
which airports have the greatest need for additional capacity.71 Within the SW Study Area  , airports in the  
following metropolitan areas were included in the evaluation:  
• Los Angeles—  Bob Hope Airport  (BUR), Long Beach -Daugherty Field Airport (LGB), Los Angeles  
International Airport (LAX), Ontario International Airport (ONT), Palm Springs International Airport  
(PSP), John Wayne-Orange County Airport (SNA)  
• San Diego—San Diego International Airport (SAN)  
• San Francisco—Metropolitan Oakland International  (OAK), San Francisco International  Airport (SFO),  
and Mineta San Jose International  Airport (SJC)  
• Las Vegas—McCarran International Airport  (LAS)  
• Phoenix—Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport (PHX)  
• Tucson—Tucson International Airport (TUS)  
The FACT 2 analysis considered planned improvements affecting runway capacity for  2015 and 2025. The  
planned improvements include new or extended runways, new or revised air traffic control procedures,  
airspace redesign, and other assumptions.  
Based on the capacity improvement assumptions, the FACT 2 analysis identifies airports that will need  
additional capacity in three broad groupings: (1) airports that would need additional capacity in 2015 after  
planned improvements; (2) airports that would need additional capacity in 2015 if planned improvements do  
not occur; and (3) airports that would need additional capacity in 2025 after planned improvements. The  
results of the FACT 2 analysis for the states in the SW S tudy Area included in the analysis are shown  in Figure  
16.  
The FACT 2 analysis indicates that airports in San Francisco and Los Angeles would need additional capacity by  
2015 even after planned improvements are in place. In the San Francisco Bay Area, specifically OAK, the  
geography, terrain,  and airspace issues will  continue to constrain this airport. These  issues limit the airport’s
texts.68:
## [PDF page 38]
ability to add runway capacity,  and the FACT 2 analysis suggests that a regional solution in conjunction with  
other airports in the Bay Area may be needed. In  Los Angeles,  LGB and SNA bo th have operational and noise  
restrictions that limit the number of operations at these facilities. If  these restrictions remain in place, the  
operational levels forecasted for these airports in 2015 will likely not be reached. Thus ,  the actual future delays  
will likely be less than the criteria established for the FACT 2 analysis. However, this may mean that significant  
demand will go unsatisfied.  
If planned improvements in all three states do not occur by 2015, airports in Tucson  and Las Vegas will  
similarly be in need of additional capacity. By 2025, San Diego and Phoenix airports will also need additional  
capacity. While geography, terrain, airfield,  and airspace issues will continue to constrain airports like SAN and  
SFO, SAN is continuing to investigate capacity enhancements and estimates the airport will exceed its  
operational capacity before the 2025 planning period. SFO has similar constraints and is participating in a  
regional planning effort to address capacity needs within the Bay Area. In 2013, SAN also completed an  
expansion of Terminal 2 to include more gates and passenger facilities.
71 FAA, Future Airport Capacity Task (FACT 2) Capacity Needs in the National Airspace System 2007-2025, May 2007

3.2.2  Air network constraints  
Constraints are prevalent and growing at airports in the SW Study  Area. One indicator of the  challenges faced  
by airports is on-time arrival performance. In this category, five major airports located in the SW Study Area  
(San Francisco, Los Angeles, San Diego, Las Vegas,  and Phoenix) are plagued by delayed arrivals ranging from  
18  percent in Phoenix to more than 30 percent in San Francisco.70 Figure 15 shows how these five airports  
(represented by orange bars) compare with other major airports in the  U.S. Although issues relating to delay  
are more severe at many of the major airports on the east coast, the physical constraints of the region’s  
airports combined with the projected growth in air travel in the Southwest  make this a notably  acute issue in  
the study area.  Additionally, the growing  security demands of air travel may affect modal choice  .

3.2.3  Currently planned air improvements  
The Federal Aviation Administration’s  (FAA) Future Airport Capacity Needs in the National Airspace System  
2007-  2025 (FACT 2) report assessed  the future capacity of 56 airports in the U.S.  ,  with a goal to determine  
which airports have the greatest need for additional capacity.71 Within the SW Study Area  , airports in the  
following metropolitan areas were included in the evaluation:  
• Los Angeles—  Bob Hope Airport  (BUR), Long Beach -Daugherty Field Airport (LGB), Los Angeles  
International Airport (LAX), Ontario International Airport (ONT), Palm Springs International Airport  
(PSP), John Wayne-Orange County Airport (SNA)  
• San Diego—San Diego International Airport (SAN)  
• San Francisco—Metropolitan Oakland International  (OAK), San Francisco International  Airport (SFO),  
and Mineta San Jose International  Airport (SJC)  
• Las Vegas—McCarran International Airport  (LAS)  
• Phoenix—Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport (PHX)  
• Tucson—Tucson International Airport (TUS)  
The FACT 2 analysis considered planned improvements affecting runway capacity for  2015 and 2025. The  
planned improvements include new or extended runways, new or revised air traffic control procedures,  
airspace redesign, and other assumptions.  
Based on the capacity improvement assumptions, the FACT 2 analysis identifies airports that will need  
additional capacity in three broad groupings: (1) airports that would need additional capacity in 2015 after  
planned improvements; (2) airports that would need additional capacity in 2015 if planned improvements do  
not occur; and (3) airports that would need additional capacity in 2025 after planned improvements. The  
results of the FACT 2 analysis for the states in the SW S tudy Area included in the analysis are shown  in Figure  
16.  
The FACT 2 analysis indicates that airports in San Francisco and Los Angeles would need additional capacity by  
2015 even after planned improvements are in place. In the San Francisco Bay Area, specifically OAK, the  
geography, terrain,  and airspace issues will  continue to constrain this airport. These  issues limit the airport’s  

## [PDF page 38]
ability to add runway capacity,  and the FACT 2 analysis suggests that a regional solution in conjunction with  
other airports in the Bay Area may be needed. In  Los Angeles,  LGB and SNA bo th have operational and noise  
restrictions that limit the number of operations at these facilities. If  these restrictions remain in place, the  
operational levels forecasted for these airports in 2015 will likely not be reached. Thus ,  the actual future delays  
will likely be less than the criteria established for the FACT 2 analysis. However, this may mean that significant  
demand will go unsatisfied.  
If planned improvements in all three states do not occur by 2015, airports in Tucson  and Las Vegas will  
similarly be in need of additional capacity. By 2025, San Diego and Phoenix airports will also need additional  
capacity. While geography, terrain, airfield,  and airspace issues will continue to constrain airports like SAN and  
SFO, SAN is continuing to investigate capacity enhancements and estimates the airport will exceed its  
operational capacity before the 2025 planning period. SFO has similar constraints and is participating in a  
regional planning effort to address capacity needs within the Bay Area. In 2013, SAN also completed an  
expansion of Terminal 2 to include more gates and passenger facilities.

## Los Angeles International Airport Quick Answers
How many passengers use LAX each day?  
About 202,000 on average. LAX handled 73.71 million passengers in 2025, which works out to roughly 201,900 a day.
How many flights take off and land at LAX each day?  
About 1,590. LAX recorded 580,996 aircraft operations (takeoffs and landings) in 2025, or roughly 1,592 a day.
What is the busiest month at LAX?  
July. In 2025, July was the busiest month with 7.18 million passengers, while February was the quietest with 4.91 million.
Which is the busiest terminal at LAX?  
The Tom Bradley International Terminal, which handled 14.09 million passengers in 2025, about 19% of the airport's total.
Has LAX recovered to pre-pandemic traffic levels?  
Not yet. The 73.71 million passengers in 2025 were about 16% below the record 88.07 million set in 2019.
How busy is LAX in 2026 so far?  
LAX handled 48.92 million passengers from January to August 2026, 1.46% fewer than in the same period of 2025.
Which airline carries the most passengers at LAX?  
Delta Air Lines, with 18.9% of LAX passengers in 2025 (13.92 million), ahead of United Airlines (16.1%) and American Airlines (15.3%).

## Los Angeles International Airport Quick Answers
How many passengers use LAX each day?  
About 202,000 on average. LAX handled 73.71 million passengers in 2025, which works out to roughly 201,900 a day.
How many flights take off and land at LAX each day?  
About 1,590. LAX recorded 580,996 aircraft operations (takeoffs and landings) in 2025, or roughly 1,592 a day.
What is the busiest month at LAX?  
July. In 2025, July was the busiest month with 7.18 million passengers, while February was the quietest with 4.91 million.
Which is the busiest terminal at LAX?  
The Tom Bradley International Terminal, which handled 14.09 million passengers in 2025, about 19% of the airport's total.
Has LAX recovered to pre-pandemic traffic levels?  
Not yet. The 73.71 million passengers in 2025 were about 16% below the record 88.07 million set in 2019.
How busy is LAX in 2026 so far?  
LAX handled 48.92 million passengers from January to August 2026, 1.46% fewer than in the same period of 2025.
Which airline carries the most passengers at LAX?  
Delta Air Lines, with 18.9% of LAX passengers in 2025 (13.92 million), ahead of United Airlines (16.1%) and American Airlines (15.3%).

## Los Angeles International Airport Quick Answers
How many passengers use LAX each day?  
About 202,000 on average. LAX handled 73.71 million passengers in 2025, which works out to roughly 201,900 a day.
How many flights take off and land at LAX each day?  
About 1,590. LAX recorded 580,996 aircraft operations (takeoffs and landings) in 2025, or roughly 1,592 a day.
What is the busiest month at LAX?  
July. In 2025, July was the busiest month with 7.18 million passengers, while February was the quietest with 4.91 million.
Which is the busiest terminal at LAX?  
The Tom Bradley International Terminal, which handled 14.09 million passengers in 2025, about 19% of the airport's total.
Has LAX recovered to pre-pandemic traffic levels?  
Not yet. The 73.71 million passengers in 2025 were about 16% below the record 88.07 million set in 2019.
How busy is LAX in 2026 so far?  
LAX handled 48.92 million passengers from January to August 2026, 1.46% fewer than in the same period of 2025.
Which airline carries the most passengers at LAX?  
Delta Air Lines, with 18.9% of LAX passengers in 2025 (13.92 million), ahead of United Airlines (16.1%) and American Airlines (15.3%).

## Los Angeles International Airport Quick Answers
How many passengers use LAX each day?  
About 202,000 on average. LAX handled 73.71 million passengers in 2025, which works out to roughly 201,900 a day.
How many flights take off and land at LAX each day?  
About 1,590. LAX recorded 580,996 aircraft operations (takeoffs and landings) in 2025, or roughly 1,592 a day.
What is the busiest month at LAX?  
July. In 2025, July was the busiest month with 7.18 million passengers, while February was the quietest with 4.91 million.
Which is the busiest terminal at LAX?  
The Tom Bradley International Terminal, which handled 14.09 million passengers in 2025, about 19% of the airport's total.
Has LAX recovered to pre-pandemic traffic levels?  
Not yet. The 73.71 million passengers in 2025 were about 16% below the record 88.07 million set in 2019.
How busy is LAX in 2026 so far?  
LAX handled 48.92 million passengers from January to August 2026, 1.46% fewer than in the same period of 2025.
Which airline carries the most passengers at LAX?  
Delta Air Lines, with 18.9% of LAX passengers in 2025 (13.92 million), ahead of United Airlines (16.1%) and American Airlines (15.3%).

## [PDF page 37]
3.2.2  Air network constraints  
Constraints are prevalent and growing at airports in the SW Study  Area. One indicator of the  challenges faced  
by airports is on-time arrival performance. In this category, five major airports located in the SW Study Area  
(San Francisco, Los Angeles, San Diego, Las Vegas,  and Phoenix) are plagued by delayed arrivals ranging from  
18  percent in Phoenix to more than 30 percent in San Francisco.70 Figure 15 shows how these five airports  
(represented by orange bars) compare with other major airports in the  U.S. Although issues relating to delay  
are more severe at many of the major airports on the east coast, the physical constraints of the region’s  
airports combined with the projected growth in air travel in the Southwest  make this a notably  acute issue in  
the study area.  Additionally, the growing  security demands of air travel may affect modal choice  .
Figure 15 Percent of flights delayed  at 29 major airports
Source: Ranking of Major Airport On-  Time Arrival Performance Year-to-Date through July 2011, Bureau of  
Transportation Statistics, http://www.bts.gov/  
programs/airline_information/airline_ontime_tables/2011_07/html/table_04.html  (data retrieved  October 2011)
70 The three primary causes of late arrivals at the five largest airports in the Southwest (LAS, LAX, PHX, SAN, and SFO) are late arriving aircraft, national  
aviation system delays, and air carrier delays.  These three causes combined account for 90-93 percent of all delays at these five airports.
Technical Background Report |  37
PDF link

## [PDF page 38]
3.2.3  Currently planned air improvements  
The Federal Aviation Administration’s  (FAA) Future Airport Capacity Needs in the National Airspace System  
2007-  2025 (FACT 2) report assessed  the future capacity of 56 airports in the U.S.  ,  with a goal to determine  
which airports have the greatest need for additional capacity.71 Within the SW Study Area  , airports in the  
following metropolitan areas were included in the evaluation:  
• Los Angeles—  Bob Hope Airport  (BUR), Long Beach -Daugherty Field Airport (LGB), Los Angeles  
International Airport (LAX), Ontario International Airport (ONT), Palm Springs International Airport  
(PSP), John Wayne-Orange County Airport (SNA)  
• San Diego—San Diego International Airport (SAN)  
• San Francisco—Metropolitan Oakland International  (OAK), San Francisco International  Airport (SFO),  
and Mineta San Jose International  Airport (SJC)  
• Las Vegas—McCarran International Airport  (LAS)  
• Phoenix—Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport (PHX)  
• Tucson—Tucson International Airport (TUS)  
The FACT 2 analysis considered planned improvements affecting runway capacity for  2015 and 2025. The  
planned improvements include new or extended runways, new or revised air traffic control procedures,  
airspace redesign, and other assumptions.  
Based on the capacity improvement assumptions, the FACT 2 analysis identifies airports that will need  
additional capacity in three broad groupings: (1) airports that would need additional capacity in 2015 after  
planned improvements; (2) airports that would need additional capacity in 2015 if planned improvements do  
not occur; and (3) airports that would need additional capacity in 2025 after planned improvements. The  
results of the FACT 2 analysis for the states in the SW S tudy Area included in the analysis are shown  in Figure  
16.  
The FACT 2 analysis indicates that airports in San Francisco and Los Angeles would need additional capacity by  
2015 even after planned improvements are in place. In the San Francisco Bay Area, specifically OAK, the  
geography, terrain,  and airspace issues will  continue to constrain this airport. These  issues limit the airport’s  

## [PDF page 38]
ability to add runway capacity,  and the FACT 2 analysis suggests that a regional solution in conjunction with  
other airports in the Bay Area may be needed. In  Los Angeles,  LGB and SNA bo th have operational and noise  
restrictions that limit the number of operations at these facilities. If  these restrictions remain in place, the  
operational levels forecasted for these airports in 2015 will likely not be reached. Thus ,  the actual future delays  
will likely be less than the criteria established for the FACT 2 analysis. However, this may mean that significant  
demand will go unsatisfied.  
If planned improvements in all three states do not occur by 2015, airports in Tucson  and Las Vegas will  
similarly be in need of additional capacity. By 2025, San Diego and Phoenix airports will also need additional  
capacity. While geography, terrain, airfield,  and airspace issues will continue to constrain airports like SAN and  
SFO, SAN is continuing to investigate capacity enhancements and estimates the airport will exceed its  
operational capacity before the 2025 planning period. SFO has similar constraints and is participating in a  
regional planning effort to address capacity needs within the Bay Area. In 2013, SAN also completed an  
expansion of Terminal 2 to include more gates and passenger facilities.
71 FAA, Future Airport Capacity Task (FACT 2) Capacity Needs in the National Airspace System 2007-2025, May 2007

## Los Angeles International Airport Quick Answers
How many passengers use LAX each day?  
About 202,000 on average. LAX handled 73.71 million passengers in 2025, which works out to roughly 201,900 a day.
How many flights take off and land at LAX each day?  
About 1,590. LAX recorded 580,996 aircraft operations (takeoffs and landings) in 2025, or roughly 1,592 a day.
What is the busiest month at LAX?  
July. In 2025, July was the busiest month with 7.18 million passengers, while February was the quietest with 4.91 million.
Which is the busiest terminal at LAX?  
The Tom Bradley International Terminal, which handled 14.09 million passengers in 2025, about 19% of the airport's total.
Has LAX recovered to pre-pandemic traffic levels?  
Not yet. The 73.71 million passengers in 2025 were about 16% below the record 88.07 million set in 2019.
How busy is LAX in 2026 so far?  
LAX handled 48.92 million passengers from January to August 2026, 1.46% fewer than in the same period of 2025.
Which airline carries the most passengers at LAX?  
Delta Air Lines, with 18.9% of LAX passengers in 2025 (13.92 million), ahead of United Airlines (16.1%) and American Airlines (15.3%).

## [PDF page 37]
3.2.2  Air network constraints  
Constraints are prevalent and growing at airports in the SW Study  Area. One indicator of the  challenges faced  
by airports is on-time arrival performance. In this category, five major airports located in the SW Study Area  
(San Francisco, Los Angeles, San Diego, Las Vegas,  and Phoenix) are plagued by delayed arrivals ranging from  
18  percent in Phoenix to more than 30 percent in San Francisco.70 Figure 15 shows how these five airports  
(represented by orange bars) compare with other major airports in the  U.S. Although issues relating to delay  
are more severe at many of the major airports on the east coast, the physical constraints of the region’s  
airports combined with the projected growth in air travel in the Southwest  make this a notably  acute issue in  
the study area.  Additionally, the growing  security demands of air travel may affect modal choice  .
Figure 15 Percent of flights delayed  at 29 major airports
Source: Ranking of Major Airport On-  Time Arrival Performance Year-to-Date through July 2011, Bureau of  
Transportation Statistics, http://www.bts.gov/  
programs/airline_information/airline_ontime_tables/2011_07/html/table_04.html  (data retrieved  October 2011)
70 The three primary causes of late arrivals at the five largest airports in the Southwest (LAS, LAX, PHX, SAN, and SFO) are late arriving aircraft, national  
aviation system delays, and air carrier delays.  These three causes combined account for 90-93 percent of all delays at these five airports.

## [PDF page 38]
3.2.3  Currently planned air improvements  
The Federal Aviation Administration’s  (FAA) Future Airport Capacity Needs in the National Airspace System  
2007-  2025 (FACT 2) report assessed  the future capacity of 56 airports in the U.S.  ,  with a goal to determine  
which airports have the greatest need for additional capacity.71 Within the SW Study Area  , airports in the  
following metropolitan areas were included in the evaluation:  
• Los Angeles—  Bob Hope Airport  (BUR), Long Beach -Daugherty Field Airport (LGB), Los Angeles  
International Airport (LAX), Ontario International Airport (ONT), Palm Springs International Airport  
(PSP), John Wayne-Orange County Airport (SNA)  
• San Diego—San Diego International Airport (SAN)  
• San Francisco—Metropolitan Oakland International  (OAK), San Francisco International  Airport (SFO),  
and Mineta San Jose International  Airport (SJC)  
• Las Vegas—McCarran International Airport  (LAS)  
• Phoenix—Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport (PHX)  
• Tucson—Tucson International Airport (TUS)  
The FACT 2 analysis considered planned improvements affecting runway capacity for  2015 and 2025. The  
planned improvements include new or extended runways, new or revised air traffic control procedures,  
airspace redesign, and other assumptions.  
Based on the capacity improvement assumptions, the FACT 2 analysis identifies airports that will need  
additional capacity in three broad groupings: (1) airports that would need additional capacity in 2015 after  
planned improvements; (2) airports that would need additional capacity in 2015 if planned improvements do  
not occur; and (3) airports that would need additional capacity in 2025 after planned improvements. The  
results of the FACT 2 analysis for the states in the SW S tudy Area included in the analysis are shown  in Figure  
16.  
The FACT 2 analysis indicates that airports in San Francisco and Los Angeles would need additional capacity by  
2015 even after planned improvements are in place. In the San Francisco Bay Area, specifically OAK, the  
geography, terrain,  and airspace issues will  continue to constrain this airport. These  issues limit the airport’s
texts.68:
## [PDF page 38]
ability to add runway capacity,  and the FACT 2 analysis suggests that a regional solution in conjunction with  
other airports in the Bay Area may be needed. In  Los Angeles,  LGB and SNA bo th have operational and noise  
restrictions that limit the number of operations at these facilities. If  these restrictions remain in place, the  
operational levels forecasted for these airports in 2015 will likely not be reached. Thus ,  the actual future delays  
will likely be less than the criteria established for the FACT 2 analysis. However, this may mean that significant  
demand will go unsatisfied.  
If planned improvements in all three states do not occur by 2015, airports in Tucson  and Las Vegas will  
similarly be in need of additional capacity. By 2025, San Diego and Phoenix airports will also need additional  
capacity. While geography, terrain, airfield,  and airspace issues will continue to constrain airports like SAN and  
SFO, SAN is continuing to investigate capacity enhancements and estimates the airport will exceed its  
operational capacity before the 2025 planning period. SFO has similar constraints and is participating in a  
regional planning effort to address capacity needs within the Bay Area. In 2013, SAN also completed an  
expansion of Terminal 2 to include more gates and passenger facilities.
71 FAA, Future Airport Capacity Task (FACT 2) Capacity Needs in the National Airspace System 2007-2025, May 2007

## Los Angeles International Airport Quick Answers
How many passengers use LAX each day?  
About 202,000 on average. LAX handled 73.71 million passengers in 2025, which works out to roughly 201,900 a day.
How many flights take off and land at LAX each day?  
About 1,590. LAX recorded 580,996 aircraft operations (takeoffs and landings) in 2025, or roughly 1,592 a day.
What is the busiest month at LAX?  
July. In 2025, July was the busiest month with 7.18 million passengers, while February was the quietest with 4.91 million.
Which is the busiest terminal at LAX?  
The Tom Bradley International Terminal, which handled 14.09 million passengers in 2025, about 19% of the airport's total.
Has LAX recovered to pre-pandemic traffic levels?  
Not yet. The 73.71 million passengers in 2025 were about 16% below the record 88.07 million set in 2019.
How busy is LAX in 2026 so far?  
LAX handled 48.92 million passengers from January to August 2026, 1.46% fewer than in the same period of 2025.
Which airline carries the most passengers at LAX?  
Delta Air Lines, with 18.9% of LAX passengers in 2025 (13.92 million), ahead of United Airlines (16.1%) and American Airlines (15.3%).

3.2.2  Air network constraints  
Constraints are prevalent and growing at airports in the SW Study  Area. One indicator of the  challenges faced  
by airports is on-time arrival performance. In this category, five major airports located in the SW Study Area  
(San Francisco, Los Angeles, San Diego, Las Vegas,  and Phoenix) are plagued by delayed arrivals ranging from  
18  percent in Phoenix to more than 30 percent in San Francisco.70 Figure 15 shows how these five airports  
(represented by orange bars) compare with other major airports in the  U.S. Although issues relating to delay  
are more severe at many of the major airports on the east coast, the physical constraints of the region’s  
airports combined with the projected growth in air travel in the Southwest  make this a notably  acute issue in  
the study area.  Additionally, the growing  security demands of air travel may affect modal choice  .

3.2.3  Currently planned air improvements  
The Federal Aviation Administration’s  (FAA) Future Airport Capacity Needs in the National Airspace System  
2007-  2025 (FACT 2) report assessed  the future capacity of 56 airports in the U.S.  ,  with a goal to determine  
which airports have the greatest need for additional capacity.71 Within the SW Study Area  , airports in the  
following metropolitan areas were included in the evaluation:  
• Los Angeles—  Bob Hope Airport  (BUR), Long Beach -Daugherty Field Airport (LGB), Los Angeles  
International Airport (LAX), Ontario International Airport (ONT), Palm Springs International Airport  
(PSP), John Wayne-Orange County Airport (SNA)  
• San Diego—San Diego International Airport (SAN)  
• San Francisco—Metropolitan Oakland International  (OAK), San Francisco International  Airport (SFO),  
and Mineta San Jose International  Airport (SJC)  
• Las Vegas—McCarran International Airport  (LAS)  
• Phoenix—Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport (PHX)  
• Tucson—Tucson International Airport (TUS)  
The FACT 2 analysis considered planned improvements affecting runway capacity for  2015 and 2025. The  
planned improvements include new or extended runways, new or revised air traffic control procedures,  
airspace redesign, and other assumptions.  
Based on the capacity improvement assumptions, the FACT 2 analysis identifies airports that will need  
additional capacity in three broad groupings: (1) airports that would need additional capacity in 2015 after  
planned improvements; (2) airports that would need additional capacity in 2015 if planned improvements do  
not occur; and (3) airports that would need additional capacity in 2025 after planned improvements. The  
results of the FACT 2 analysis for the states in the SW S tudy Area included in the analysis are shown  in Figure  
16.  
The FACT 2 analysis indicates that airports in San Francisco and Los Angeles would need additional capacity by  
2015 even after planned improvements are in place. In the San Francisco Bay Area, specifically OAK, the  
geography, terrain,  and airspace issues will  continue to constrain this airport. These  issues limit the airport’s  

## [PDF page 38]
ability to add runway capacity,  and the FACT 2 analysis suggests that a regional solution in conjunction with  
other airports in the Bay Area may be needed. In  Los Angeles,  LGB and SNA bo th have operational and noise  
restrictions that limit the number of operations at these facilities. If  these restrictions remain in place, the  
operational levels forecasted for these airports in 2015 will likely not be reached. Thus ,  the actual future delays  
will likely be less than the criteria established for the FACT 2 analysis. However, this may mean that significant  
demand will go unsatisfied.  
If planned improvements in all three states do not occur by 2015, airports in Tucson  and Las Vegas will  
similarly be in need of additional capacity. By 2025, San Diego and Phoenix airports will also need additional  
capacity. While geography, terrain, airfield,  and airspace issues will continue to constrain airports like SAN and  
SFO, SAN is continuing to investigate capacity enhancements and estimates the airport will exceed its  
operational capacity before the 2025 planning period. SFO has similar constraints and is participating in a  
regional planning effort to address capacity needs within the Bay Area. In 2013, SAN also completed an  
expansion of Terminal 2 to include more gates and passenger facilities.
